question: A continuous-time signal x(t) = cos(2*pi*1200*t) is sampled at fs = 1000 Hz. What frequency does the resulting discrete-time sequence appear to have when reconstructed by an ideal lowpass filter at fs/2?
reference_answer: 200 Hz. The signal at 1200 Hz is above the Nyquist frequency of 500 Hz, so it aliases. The apparent frequency is |1200 - 1000| = 200 Hz, which lies in the baseband 0-500 Hz.
must_include: 200 Hz
exceeds the Nyquist frequency of 500 Hz
aliasing

question: A student writes: 'My DFT of a 64-sample record didn't resolve the two tones, so I zero-padded to 1024 points. Now the peaks are separated, which proves zero-padding improved my frequency resolution.' Is the student right? Explain.
reference_answer: No. Frequency resolution is set by the length of the observed record, T = N*Ts, not by the DFT length. Zero-padding interpolates the DTFT more finely — it draws a smoother curve through the same underlying spectrum — but adds no new information and cannot separate tones the record length cannot resolve. If the padded plot appears to show two peaks, they were already resolvable at 64 points; genuinely unresolved tones remain a single smeared lobe however much padding is applied. To improve resolution, observe for longer.
must_include: resolution is set by the record duration T = N*Ts
zero-padding interpolates the spectrum
adds no new information
observe the signal for longer to improve resolution

question: H(z) = 1 / (1 - 0.5*z^-1). Give the region of convergence for the causal case and state whether that system is BIBO stable.
reference_answer: There is a single pole at z = 0.5. For the causal case the ROC is the region outside the outermost pole, |z| > 0.5. The ROC includes the unit circle, so the system is BIBO stable. (The anticausal case, ROC |z| < 0.5, excludes the unit circle and is unstable — the transfer function alone does not determine stability without the ROC.)
must_include: pole at z = 0.5
ROC is |z| > 0.5 for the causal case
the ROC contains the unit circle
BIBO stable
must_not_include: ROC is |z| < 0.5 for the causal case
stability follows from the transfer function alone

question: Show why an FIR filter with a real, symmetric impulse response h[n] = h[N-1-n] has exactly linear phase.
reference_answer: Write H(e^jw) = sum_{n=0}^{N-1} h[n] e^{-jwn}. Pair term n with term N-1-n and factor out e^{-jw(N-1)/2}. Using the symmetry h[n] = h[N-1-n], each pair combines into a cosine, giving H(e^jw) = e^{-jw(N-1)/2} * A(w) where A(w) is real-valued. The phase is therefore -w(N-1)/2 — linear in w — with jumps of pi wherever A(w) changes sign. The group delay is the constant (N-1)/2 samples, so every frequency component is delayed equally and no phase distortion is introduced.
must_include: factor out e^{-jw(N-1)/2}
the remaining amplitude term A(w) is real
phase is -w(N-1)/2, linear in w
constant group delay of (N-1)/2 samples
must_not_include: only IIR filters can have linear phase

question: Why is the periodogram not a consistent estimator of the power spectral density, and what does Welch's method change?
reference_answer: The periodogram's variance does not decrease as the record length N grows — at each frequency it stays on the order of the true PSD squared, so lengthening the record adds frequencies but does not reduce the scatter at any one of them. It is asymptotically unbiased but inconsistent. Welch's method divides the record into overlapping windowed segments, computes a periodogram of each, and averages them. Averaging K roughly independent estimates cuts the variance by about a factor of K, at the cost of coarser frequency resolution because each segment is shorter — the standard bias-variance trade.
must_include: variance does not decrease with increasing N
inconsistent estimator
averaging periodograms of overlapping segments reduces variance
resolution is traded away because segments are shorter
must_not_include: Welch's method improves both variance and resolution
